09aa95c7bdeb5ba47970ef47eec3122bf1e1c38a.name: Standard
09aa95c7bdeb5ba47970ef47eec3122bf1e1c38a.summary: The most widely used signer contract. Open to everyone, can pay rewards to a Bitcoin address, and the pool sets its own fee.
09aa95c7bdeb5ba47970ef47eec3122bf1e1c38a.detail: This is the reference contract most pools run unchanged. It turns nobody away: anyone can stake with a pool using it, without an invitation. If you give it a Bitcoin address when you stake, it remembers it and your rewards go to Bitcoin rather than arriving as sBTC on Stacks. Each pool running it sets its own fee and can change that fee later.

1b7c3674ac0dbb5da092b5e2e07684c06c7079cf.name: Standard (changed ABI)
1b7c3674ac0dbb5da092b5e2e07684c06c7079cf.summary: The Standard contract with one function's answer changed. Open to everyone, and can pay rewards to a Bitcoin address.
1b7c3674ac0dbb5da092b5e2e07684c06c7079cf.detail: The build the Xverse signers run. For anyone staking it behaves like the Standard contract: open to everyone, and rewards can go to a Bitcoin address. What differs is the interface, not the behaviour — when it pays a staker out it reports only the amount, where the Standard contract also reports the Bitcoin withdrawal it opened. Anything reading that answer has to know which of the two it is talking to, so it is listed on its own rather than folded into Standard.

d5718c4d8771628da0a24e4345534b4c9ec630f7.name: Invite-only
d5718c4d8771628da0a24e4345534b4c9ec630f7.summary: A small signer contract where the operator chooses who may join. Rewards arrive as sBTC on Stacks.
d5718c4d8771628da0a24e4345534b4c9ec630f7.detail: A short contract that checks you against a list the operator controls before letting you stake. If you are not on it, staking is refused. It has no Bitcoin payout option, so rewards arrive as sBTC on Stacks, and it carries no fee of its own — which does not mean staking is free, because a fee may be taken elsewhere.

8925fa8554e7d42ccce00f760b26d31d6c672a9a.name: Native Pool
8925fa8554e7d42ccce00f760b26d31d6c672a9a.summary: You join through the Native Pool contract rather than pox-5 staking directly. Rewards arrive as sBTC on Stacks.
8925fa8554e7d42ccce00f760b26d31d6c672a9a.detail: This signer only accepts you if you join through the Native Pool contract, so you sign up there rather than staking with the signer directly. Rewards arrive as sBTC on Stacks. It carries no fee of its own.

d6c5e82af733250d80b38be57d02c5ff6677ec27.name: Capped Fee
d6c5e82af733250d80b38be57d02c5ff6677ec27.summary: Open to everyone, can pay rewards to a Bitcoin address, and the fee can never go above 5% — with a month’s warning before any rise.
d6c5e82af733250d80b38be57d02c5ff6677ec27.detail: Open to everyone, with no invitation needed, and it can pay your rewards to a Bitcoin address as well as sBTC on Stacks. What sets it apart is that it has advantageous rules for the users. The fee can never exceed 5% however the operator behaves, because the contract refuses a higher one. A rise in the fee has to be queued two reward cycles ahead, roughly a month, so you have time to move before it applies — a cut takes effect at once. You can also change where your Bitcoin goes, and the smallest payout you will accept.

2aea99cfe42ccb9b9dd541d34c21cd852c5726f1.name: Juice Pool
2aea99cfe42ccb9b9dd541d34c21cd852c5726f1.summary: Open to everyone and pays rewards as sBTC on Stacks. Fee changes have to be announced before they take effect, and stakers the pool marks as OG pay no fee at all.
2aea99cfe42ccb9b9dd541d34c21cd852c5726f1.detail: Open to everyone, with no invitation needed. Rewards arrive as sBTC on Stacks rather than to a Bitcoin address. Two things set it apart: the operator can pause new staking, and a change of fee has to be proposed first and confirmed in a second step, so it cannot change without warning. It also keeps a list of stakers it calls OG, who are charged no fee at all however high the fee goes for everyone else. The pool decides who is on that list and can take someone off it again, so being OG is a discount in the pool’s gift rather than something the contract promises you.

5fde076339b4920d38de1d8f34ea518cf68380b7.name: Invite-only (with btc address)
5fde076339b4920d38de1d8f34ea518cf68380b7.summary: A small signer contract where the operator chooses who may stake. It takes a Bitcoin address from you and stores it, but pays nothing to it: every reward leaves as sBTC, in one payment to one address the operator sets.
5fde076339b4920d38de1d8f34ea518cf68380b7.detail:
The operator keeps a list of who may stake with this contract. If you are not on it, staking is refused, so this is not a pool you can join by deciding to. Only pox-5 itself can ask the contract whether a stake is allowed, and the list is the only question it asks about you.

When you stake it will take a Bitcoin address from you, check that it is a real one, and store it under your name where anyone can read it. Nothing in the contract ever pays to that address. Claiming a cycle sends the whole of its sBTC to a single recipient the operator sets, and there is no function here that pays an individual staker at all — so what the address is for is being read: a pool that hands out rewards itself can look up every address it has been given and send Bitcoin to it. Recording yours is how you tell the pool where you want to be paid, not something the contract will do for you.

That is the thing to understand about staking here. Both halves of what you get — how much, and in what — are decided by the pool after the rewards have left this contract, so they rest on what the operator has agreed with you rather than on anything the code will enforce. It takes no fee of its own, which says less than it would elsewhere: the rewards do not pass through it on their way to you.

abd7d55c747dee025ceb9e29a177cc9b4906b018.name: Trustful rewards
abd7d55c747dee025ceb9e29a177cc9b4906b018.summary: Open to anyone, and it will not let you stake without giving it a Bitcoin address. Every reward it claims becomes the operator’s to withdraw: no function in it pays a staker, so what reaches you is whatever the pool sends you afterwards.
abd7d55c747dee025ceb9e29a177cc9b4906b018.detail:
Anyone may stake with this contract. It asks nothing about who you are but it will refuse the stake if you do not hand it a Bitcoin address. It checks the address is a real one and stores it under your name, where anyone can read it back.

When a cycle’s rewards are claimed, the whole of the sBTC is added to a single balance the contract calls its earned fees, and an operator can withdraw any part of that to any recipient they choose. There is no function here that pays an individual staker, and no record of what any staker is owed — the contract does not keep books on you at all. Its own comment says the withdrawal is for bridging and off-chain distribution, which is an accurate description of where the money goes and of who is holding it when it gets there.

So the address you gave it is for reading, not for paying: a pool that hands out rewards itself can look up every address it has been given and send Bitcoin to each one. Recording yours is how you tell the pool where you want to be paid. Whether you are paid, and how much of the cycle you get, is not a thing this code decides.

That is what separates it from the other contracts here. Most of them take a fee and pass the rest on, so the fee is the part you have to trust and the remainder is the part the code guarantees. This one has no fee to read, because the distinction does not exist inside it: the rewards arrive in one pot and leave by one door. Everything about what you get rests on your agreement with the operator rather than on anything that can be checked on chain.

It also refuses protocol bonds, so no Bitcoin L1 can be locked. STX staking is all it does.

b52f096114ec55623aa82dde6b89a6849107e42c.name: Trustful rewards (1000 STX minimum)
b52f096114ec55623aa82dde6b89a6849107e42c.summary: The Trustful rewards contract with a floor: you cannot stake less than 1000 STX. Everything else is the same as Trustful Rewards contract. It takes a Bitcoin address, and every reward it claims becomes the operator’s to withdraw and distribute.
b52f096114ec55623aa82dde6b89a6849107e42c.detail:
This is the Trustful rewards contract with one line added, and the line is a minimum: a stake of less than 1000 STX is refused. The floor is on the position rather than on the top-up, so an existing staker adding to a smaller lock is refused as well until the total clears it. Nothing else about who may join has changed — there is no list and no invitation, so anyone with 1000 STX may stake.

The rest is identical. Staking is refused unless you hand over a Bitcoin address, which the contract checks and stores under your name for anyone to read back. When a cycle is claimed, the whole of its sBTC is added to one balance, and an operator can withdraw any part of it to any recipient. No function pays an individual staker, and no record is kept of what any staker is owed.

So the address is for reading rather than for paying: it is how you tell the pool where to send Bitcoin. There is no fee to compare against other pools, because the split the fee describes does not happen in here — the rewards arrive in one pot and leave by one door. What you get rests on your agreement with the operator.

Protocol bonds are refused, so no Bitcoin L1 can be locked.
